latin: Impassibilitas corporum post resurrectionem erit ex pleno dominio animae super corpus.
latin_note: Farmer's apparatus records a variant: the 1486 printing reads 'domino', corrected to 'dominio' in the 1487 printing (farmer1998:11439); theses.json and this entry follow the 1487 reading.
translation: The impassibility of bodies after the resurrection will come from the soul's full dominion over the body.
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch3, from Latin at farmer1998:11433

sources.text: Thomas Aquinas, commentary on the Sentences (specific book, distinction and article not given in the excerpt consulted)
sources.pico_relation: Edelheit discusses the thesis in connection with Thomas's commentary on the Sentences without the excerpt naming the precise locus

doctrine: The thesis explains the impassibility (incapacity for suffering) of resurrected bodies as an effect of the soul's complete dominion over the body (edelheit2022:10916). Farmer's note ties the same issue to the debate over Christ's own impassibility discussed at thesis 4.12 (from Scotus), and situates it within Dominican-Franciscan controversy (farmer1998:11512).
context: Farmer records that the Apology (Opera, [page not given in the excerpt]) also addresses the issue, without further detail available in the sources consulted (farmer1998:11512).
historiography: Edelheit is the only scholar found discussing this thesis in the sources consulted; he treats it as continuing an examination, begun at the preceding thesis, of what happens to bodies in a non-corporeal, spiritual or miraculous condition (edelheit2022:10916).

quotations.text: It states that the incapacity of bodies for suffering after resurrection is the result of the complete dominion of the soul over the body.
